catalog_quote: Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length) Stress seems to be predictable based on tone plus rhythm of syllables within a phonological phrase. Vowel length is present, generally predictable on basis of morphology. Tone is phonemic. There is contrast between falling, rising, level, and rising-falling tones. pà 'by' pá 'split' pá 'pulverized' pâ 'tree sp.' kaù 'lizard' kaú 'betel pepper' katÚ 'rollers' kaû 'palm sp.'

new_statements.rule_in_words: Rumu is a tone (word-melody / pitch accent) language with four contrastive tonal patterns (falling, rising, level, rising-falling); stress is not contrastive and is described as predictable from the tonal pattern together with syllable rhythm inside the phonological phrase; no fixed stress position is given. (Second-hand via Cahill 2011: Newman & Petterson 1990 locate a single tone-bearing 'accented' syllable per phonological word, normally the final syllable, penultimate in about 8.5% of words.)
new_statements.exceptions: None in the OPD. Cahill 2011 (summarising Newman & Petterson 1990) reports c. 8.5% of words with the tonal accent on the penult instead of the final syllable.
new_statements.domain_note: The OPD ties stress to the phonological phrase ('rhythm of syllables within a phonological phrase'), not the word; tone is lexical/word-level. Grammar Essentials (1986:2) marks tone by an apostrophe 'in the place where the voice is highest in a word'.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the Rumu spoken at Kopi village (Kikori, Gulf Province), i.e. Rumu/Kairi/Dumu proper = rumu1243 [klq]; the 2007 dictionary flags some Sirebe-dialect forms. 'Kairi' in Newman & Petterson 1990 and Cahill 2011 is the same language (not the Ikobi-Mena 'Kairi' varieties to the west, which Petterson 1986:2 explicitly distinguishes).

tone_statements.citation: Donohue, Mark. 1997. Tone systems in New Guinea. Linguistic Typology 1(3): 347-386. doi:10.1515/lity.1997.1.3.347
tone_statements.quote: Kairi shows four tonal contrasts, between (on monosyllables) high, ris[ing,] falling, and rise-fall tones (Newman & Petterson 1989). ... Kairi shows o[nly] four: high on both syllables, low on the first and high on the seco[nd,] high on the first and low on the second, and finally low on the first and falling on the second. ... [We] must posit a rule such that the second last tone unit (H, L, H, and [L] respectively) is associated with the last tone-bearing unit (syllable) of [the w]ord; this is a fixed position for tone-assignment in the language
tone_statements.check: quotation from a journal article located by the 2026-09-24 journal search, not yet verified by a second reading
tone_statements.summary: Kairi is a word-tone language with four melodies (H, LH, HL, LHL) anchored to the final syllable, so a disyllable shows four patterns rather than nine. The entry (Rumu; it cites Newman & Petterson on Kairi) already carries this analysis via Cahill 2011.

tone_statements.citation: Newman, John F. & Robert G. Petterson. 1990. The tones of Kairi. Oceanic Linguistics 29(1): 49-76.
tone_statements.quote: Kairi has distinctive tones which function as a pitch-accent system: there is one syllable in each morpheme, described as the "accented syllable," which must have its tonal properties specified; once the accented syllable and its tone type have been specified, the tonal properties of the remaining syllables in the morpheme are assigned in a rule-governed way. [p. 49] ... The four basic tone patterns of Kairi are H (high level), LH (rising), HL (falling), and LHL (rising-falling). These are the only tone patterns which occur in monomorphemic one-syllable words. [p. 50] ... On the segmental tier, the star only occurs over the last syllable; on the tonal tier, the star only occurs over the second tone of the basic tone pattern. [p. 57] ... The accented syllable would normally be associated with a change in pitch and in the case of Kairi this means the last syllable in all the words discussed so far, except those which have a H tone throughout. [p. 58] ... The one accented syllable in each word is marked with a diacritic. Words which have no pitch change have no accented syllable and consequently no diacritic. [p. 59]
